topic: Expansion of Products of Two Linear Binomials using Distributive Law

lessonData.topic: Expansion of Products of Two Linear Binomials using Distributive Law
lessonData.subject: Mathematics
lessonData.tagline: Unlock the power of double distribution: every term pairs up!
lessonData.overview: Expanding two linear binomials requires applying the distributive law so that every term in the first bracket multiplies every term in the second bracket. By keeping track of negative signs and grouping expressions inside brackets during subtraction, you can expand and simplify expressions accurately without dropping crucial cross terms.

diagram.description: Visualizing how two linear factors break down into four distinct products before simplification.

nodes.label: First Binomial Split
nodes.sublabel: Separate into terms a and b
nodes.details: Split the first factor (a + b) into two separate multipliers, 'a' and 'b', each acting on the second bracket.

nodes.details: Multiply 'a' by both terms in the second bracket, yielding two partial products: ac and ad.

nodes.label: Distribute Second Term: b(c + d)
nodes.details: Multiply 'b' by both terms in the second bracket, yielding two partial products: bc and bd.

nodes.label: Collect All 4 Terms
nodes.details: Combine the four products, paying strict attention to positive and negative signs from the original binomials.

nodes.label: Sign Management & Like Terms
nodes.details: Group like terms together and distribute preceding negative signs across all terms within brackets.

chalkNotes.title: Expansion of Two Linear Binomials
chalkNotes.subtitle: Distributive Law & Sign Rules
chalkNotes.coreRuleOrFormula: (a + b)(c + d) = a(c + d) + b(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd
bulletPoints: Every term in the first bracket must multiply every term in the second bracket, producing 4 terms before collecting like terms.
Never multiply only first and last terms: (a + b)(c + d) is NOT equal to ac + bd.
When subtracting an expanded binomial product, keep the entire expansion inside brackets: -(ac + ad + bc + bd) = -ac - ad - bc - bd.
keyTakeaways: Double distribution guarantees that no middle/cross terms are left behind.
A negative sign in front of a bracket flips the sign of every single term inside once expanded.

quiz.question: Simplify the expression completely: 2ac - (3a - b)(c + 4b)
quiz.explanation: First, expand the product (3a - b)(c + 4b) using double distribution: 3a(c + 4b) - b(c + 4b) = 3ac + 12ab - bc - 4b^2. Second, subtract the entire bracketed expansion: 2ac - (3ac + 12ab - bc - 4b^2) = 2ac - 3ac - 12ab + bc + 4b^2. Finally, combine like terms (2ac - 3ac = -ac) to obtain 4b^2 - ac - 12ab + bc. Option 1 forgets to distribute the minus sign to -4b^2. Option 2 mistakenly multiplies only the first and last terms. Option 3 incorrectly adds 3ac instead of subtracting it.

suggestedQuestions: If someone expands (x + 2)(x + 3) as x^2 + 6, what happens when we substitute x = 1 to test their answer?
When simplifying 2ac - (3a - b)(c + 4b), why is it dangerous to remove the brackets in the very first step?
How does expanding single brackets like 3x(2y - 5) directly prepare us for expanding two binomials?

main.title: Expanding Binomials with the Area Model
main.why: It shows that multiplying two binomials is like finding the area of a rectangle, visually proving that all four terms must be calculated.
main.checkQuestion: Looking at the grid, why do we have four sections instead of just two?

steps.name: Draw the main frame
steps.caption: We represent the product (a + b)(c + d) as the total area of a rectangle.

steps.name: Label the sides
steps.caption: Split the length into 'a' and 'b', and the height into 'c' and 'd'.

steps.name: Fill the four parts
steps.caption: Each section is a product; notice how every term multiplies the others.

contrast:foil-missing-inner-outer.title: Testing the Product Rule
contrast:foil-missing-inner-outer.why: It shows that multiplying only first and last terms ignores two 'missing' areas of the rectangle, proving that the rule requires four terms.
contrast:foil-missing-inner-outer.checkQuestion: How do the red labels help explain why x² + 6 isn't the full area of the rectangle?

steps.name: Draw the area model
steps.caption: Let's represent the product (x + 2)(x + 3) as a rectangle.

steps.name: Show the partial products
steps.caption: If we multiply only the parts, we get x² + 6.

steps.name: Reveal missing pieces
steps.caption: But look at the empty gaps; the full area must include these too.

steps.name: Conclusion
steps.caption: If x=1, why does our rectangle total equal 20, but x²+6 only equal 7?

contrast:foil-missing-inner-outer.focus: Only multiplying the first terms and last terms together, i.e., $(a+b)(c+d) = ac + bd$.

contrast:drop-brackets-after-subtraction.title: The Negative Sign Trap
contrast:drop-brackets-after-subtraction.why: This visual layout exposes how a minus sign affects the entire bracketed expression, making the hidden distribution clear.
